transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2027-09-07
- Time: 15:30 PDT
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SRE); Jordan Lee, Maya Patel, Trevor Huang, Anita Rao (Nimbus Health)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on latency SLO framing (first-token vs per-token), p95/p99 targets, sampling approach for the pilot, and who owns what for the benchmark runs. Customer wants to validate both TTFT and TPOT with production-like payload variance and cold-start episodes.

Topics covered:
- Clarify TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (per-token latency+throughput) and tradeoffs
- Proposed target bands and acceptance criteria (p95/p99)
- Workload sizing: concurrency, qps, payload length distribution
- Measurement plan: traffic replay vs synthetic sweep, warm vs cold cache, sample sizes and confidence intervals
- Roles, timing, and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alicia: ok great, everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll try to keep to 40 minutes. first, quick intros?
[00:07] Jordan: yeah i'm Jordan, lead ML eng at Nimbus, we own the inference infra for the patient summarization microservice
[00:12] Maya: Maya, platform SRE, i handle networking and perf testing for the team
[00:16] Trevor: Trevor, PM, i'll own business success criteria for the pilot
[00:21] Anita: Anita, security, i'll be triaging compliance questions
[00:24] Alicia: and i'm Alicia on AE side, with Samir who's our performance SE. Samir, want to intro?
[00:29] Samir: hey all, Samir, perf SE, i run the benchmark harness and will help design the replay profiles and metrics collection
[00:35] Diego: diego from Redwood SRE, i'll own instrumenting our telemetry during pilot runs

[03:12] Jordan: our main ask is twofold: 1) how fast can you get a first token back under production payloads and 2) how does throughput scale when we hit 200–300 qps. we want clear acceptance criteria that we can put in the pilot charter
[03:28] Alicia: makes sense. to align terms: we'll be measuring TTFT (time to first token) as the latency from request arrival to first generated byte. TPOT we'll treat as average per-token generation time across the sequence, and we'll also report end-to-end per-request total latency.
[03:45] Maya: is TPOT the same as tokens-per-second inverted? sometimes our SREs think in tps not per-token ms
[03:52] Samir: yeah, you can flip it. TPOT in ms/token is convenient for model runtime profiling; ops teams sometimes prefer throughput rps. we'll report both.

[06:01] Trevor: what are realistic target numbers? like p95 TTFT under 200ms? p99 under 400ms?
[06:09] Samir: depends on model size and quantization. for a 7B quantized variant we're seeing p95 TTFT ~120–180ms on gpus we use. p99 can spike to 300–450ms with cold tails. for TPOT, p95 ms/token typically 6–12ms/token depending on sequence length.
[06:35] Jordan: ok we run mainly an instruction summarizer, avg output length 140 tokens with heavy variance (10% under 20 tokens, 40% 20–100, 50% 100–320).
[06:48] Samir: that's useful. we need the payload distribution to synthesize realistic runs. also note KV cache warm fraction matters: if 80% of requests hit a warm KV cache TTFT drops significantly. we should run both warm and cold scenarios.

[09:00] Maya: on concurrency, our prod baseline is steady 60 qps with bursts to 220 qps during batch windows. pilot should sweep 0–250 qps and hold at target plateaus for 10–15 minutes each.
[09:15] Samir: recommended sweep: baseline 60 qps, then 120, 180, 220, 250, hold for 10 minutes, collect p50/p95/p99 and token throughput. also include spike tests for 1-minute sudden bursts.

[11:37] Jordan: about measurement windows and sample size — what does Redwood require to declare an SLO pass? we don't want false positives from sampling error
[11:46] Samir: we normally require at least N=1,000 requests per target window for stable percentiles; for p99 we like 10k samples over the measurement window if feasible. we'll compute 95% confidence intervals on the percentile estimates.
[11:59] Alicia: so for the pilot acceptance, if p95 TTFT < 200ms and p99 < 400ms across the 60–220 qps range on our replay profile, then primary SLO met, subject to business signoff.

[14:03] Trevor: what about cold starts and autoscaling? our infra scales new replicas during burst and we see cold cache effects for ~20% of requests
[14:11] Diego: we can simulate cold-start episodes by cycling model workers and running a spine of cold-replay traffic. we'll record the fraction of cold requests and report cold-tail metrics separately.
[14:22] Maya: also need to validate request routing fallbacks — we have graceful degradation where heavier models are swapped with smaller ones. can Redwood simulate model variant fallbacks?
[14:30] Samir: yes, we can test the fallback policy: during overload, route 30% of traffic to a smaller model variant and measure end-user latency and quality delta. we'll include a canary rollback test.

[17:50] Jordan: about measurement fidelity: do you run on-host agents or will we see only logs from Redwood endpoints? we need raw traces for our observability stack
[17:59] Diego: we can expose stdout metrics and send traces to Nimbus's OTLP collector over an agreed peering; Samir: we'll also share our raw event logs for the run. note that transcript logs sometimes have tokenization quirks — but we'll provide both timestamped token events and aggregated histograms.

[20:03] Anita: security question — does the pilot require SOC2 docs and data residency guarantees for replayed traces? we must ensure PHI is not in test data
[20:11] Alicia: yes, send sanitized/anonymized traces. Redwood will sign DPA and we can share our SOC2 report. for private deployments we'd do VPC peering or on-prem agent. for the hosted pilot, we'll redact PII and use encryption at rest in our test buckets.

[22:44] Trevor: sampling plan — what's the recommended approach to choose tracer windows?
[22:52] Samir: three-step plan: 1) traffic clustering: cluster traces by input size and prompt pattern, create 4–5 buckets (tiny, short, median, long, extreme). 2) sample percent: choose weighted sampling to match production distribution (e.g., 10% tiny, 40% short, 30% median, 15% long, 5% extreme). 3) run both steady-state replay and load sweep on each bucket and aggregate.

[25:18] Jordan: and for p95/p99 CI, how will you report why a percentile failed? we want root cause signals
[25:26] Samir: we'll annotate percentile fail events with richer context: was the request cold, was the worker swapped, queueing depth, CPU/GPU util, memory pressure, and kernel-level stall markers. we'll include a failure heatmap.

[27:00] Maya: what harness will you use? our team prefers k6 and we have some locust scripts already
[27:07] Samir: Redwood will provide a k6 scenario that replays serialized payloads and collects per-request TTFT by instrumenting the client and server. for token-level timing we'll use our instrumented runtime that streams first-byte timestamps. we'll convert locust scripts to k6 if you prefer.

[30:10] Jordan: timeline? we want a 3-week pilot: week 0 prep, week 1 replay and smoke, week 2 full sweep and analysis, week 3 report and handoff. is that realistic?
[30:19] Alicia: yes that's our recommended cadence. to be concrete: prep (this week) — collect traces and sanitize; Redwood config and dry-run; kickoff run next week; full sweep the following week and analysis report the week after.

[32:46] Trevor: acceptance criteria recap, to put in pilot charter:
- TTFT p95 < 200ms across weighted replay distribution
- TTFT p99 < 450ms across weighted replay distribution, with documented cold-start contribution
- TPOT p95 < 12ms/token for median sequences, and aggregate throughput >= 250 tokens/sec at 220 qps workload scaled across cluster
- No single run with sustained GPU queueing > 250ms for more than 3 minutes

[33:30] Samir: we recommend an explicit measurement note: if cached warm fraction differs by >20% between replay and prod, we'll re-run after adjusting sample weights. also if p99 confidence intervals exceed ±15% we won't declare pass until more samples are collected.

[35:12] Anita: security checklist — please include DPA, SOC2, list of subprocesors, and an export control note. we'll need the docs before any data transfer.
[35:21] Alicia: noted, i'll attach SOC2 + DPA template.

[36:00] Diego: telemetry — we'll emit OTLP traces for each request with spans: client-call, model-sched, kernel-exec, token-stream. timestamps are attached to first-byte and per-token deltas.

[37:45] Jordan: edge case: multi-turn session reuse, we have many sessions that append state; KV cache hit ratio there is high and TTFT is much lower. can you emulate session-aware traffic?
[37:56] Samir: yes we'll parametrize cache-hit fraction in the harness; we'll run separate session-aware replay and include combined results.

[39:30] Trevor: final recap and owners?
[39:35] Alicia: mia, owners: Alicia send pricing and docs; Samir prepare harness and canary/fallback scenarios; Jordan provide sanitized traces and success criteria doc; Maya confirm networking. we also said kickoff run 2027-09-14.
[39:50] Jordan: sounds good.
[40:00] Anita: thanks, we'll review security checklist and ping if anything else.
[40:07] Alicia: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the repo link and scheduling invite. bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on measurement specifics (post-call free-text):
- Warm vs cold runs: define cold as worker spin-up + empty KV cache window producing first-token delay; run at least 3 cold episodes of 5 minutes each and report cold-tail contribution.%
- Percentiles: compute p95 and p99 using hdrhistogram with reservoir sampling for heavy tails; report 95% CI via bootstrap for each percentile event bin.
- Data hygiene: customer to provide sanitized traces in NDJSON with fields: request_id, timestamp, input_len, output_len, session_id|null, cache_hit_bool, prompt_type.
- Quality tradeoffs: if TPOT improvement from quantization leads to more than 3% drop in ROUGE/QA score on sample evals, flag for product review.
